result.answer:
Verdict: SUPPORTED

Evidence for: the scifact-386 abstract states that “Most errors occurred when giving bolus doses or making up drugs that required multiple step preparation” [S:54f9a179a7f0#3]. It also reports 249 IV drug errors, with at least one error in 212 of 430 IV doses (49%) [S:54f9a179a7f0#3], and its conclusion emphasizes reducing ward preparation and using technology for slow bolus administration [S:54f9a179a7f0#3]. Evidence against: none in the supplied spans.

Limitation: the supplied scifact-386 source is an abstract, not the full PDF, so it does not provide a numerical phase-by-phase distribution or a detailed step-by-step preparation breakdown [S:54f9a179a7f0#2]. It also describes intravenous drugs generally, not explicitly “peripheral” IV [S:54f9a179a7f0#2].

[5] RESULTS 249 errors were identified.
[6] At least one error occurred in 212 out of 430 intravenous drug doses (49%, 95% confidence interval
45% to 54%).
[7] Three doses (1%) had potentially severe errors, 126 (29%) potentially moderate errors, and 83 (19%)
potentially minor errors.
[8] Most errors occurred when giving bolus doses or making up drugs that required multiple step
preparation.
[9] CONCLUSIONS The rate of intravenous drug errors was high.
[10] Although most errors would cause only short term adverse effects, a few could have been serious.
[11] A combination of reducing the amount of preparation on the ward, training, and technology to
administer slow bolus doses would probably have the greatest effect on error rates.
